meta.title: V8 hidden classes (Maps) and inline caches: shapes, speculation, deopt
meta.subject: Computer science
meta.topic: V8 Maps, inline caches, speculation and deopt

story.title: Four shapes make one read 4× slower, and a deopt keeps V8 honest

tldr: V8 gives every object a hidden class (a Map) that records its layout, and every property read site an inline cache that remembers the last Map it saw. When the Map matches, a read is one compare and one load. Optimized code bets that the Map stays the same, checks it with one compare, and deoptimizes back to the interpreter when the bet loses.
why: Why it matters: property access is the most common operation in JavaScript, and the same guards that make it fast have been the source of serious browser exploits (CVE-2020-6418, CVE-2020-16009, CVE-2025-2135).

cards.title: Objects carry a shape tag, and each read remembers it
cards.brief:
JavaScript objects can gain and lose fields at any time, so a naive engine searches for x on every read. V8 tags each object with its layout (its hidden class, or Map) and each read site keeps a sticky note of the last tag it saw.

When the tag matches, the read is one fixed-offset load.

cards.title: Six things to know first
cards.brief:
• Map: V8's hidden class, the layout descriptor shared by objects built alike.
  • Inline cache: a per-site memo keyed on Map.
  • Tiers: Ignition, Sparkplug, Maglev, TurboFan.

Six in total, each defined inside.

cards.title: Every Chrome tab, Node server and Electron app runs it
cards.brief: Chrome, Node.js, Deno, Electron apps and Cloudflare Workers all run V8. You never call it; you choose stable object shapes. Watch for --trace-deopt spam or LoadIC_Megamorphic in a profile.

cards.title: "Fixed-offset loads" hides five moving parts
cards.brief: Maps form a transition tree keyed by property name and order, so {x,y} and {y,x} differ. The IC is a one-way state machine: mono, poly, mega. Optimized code bets on it and needs deopt. Every removed guard is a security assumption.

cards.title: Without shapes, every o.x is a search and every object repeats its keys
cards.brief: A naive property read is a hash probe or scan with several dependent loads, tens of nanoseconds, and each object stores its own key names. Self measured a point at 10 machine words without maps and 3 with. V8 needs about one load.

cards.title: A Map is a struct discovered at runtime
cards.brief: Map is the struct definition, the object is an instance, and the inline cache is a JIT-style switch(map) at each site. Unlike C structs, Maps mutate and get abandoned, and the switch gets baked into machine code, so invalidation is the hard part.

cards.title: One getX call, from cold miss to a deopt
cards.brief:
A literal {x,y} follows Map transitions M0 → M1 → M2. The first call misses and stores a handler; the second is a compare and a load. A call with {y,x} fails CheckMaps, deopts, and the IC goes polymorphic.

6-step trace and an IC shape simulator inside.

cards.title: A speculation pays off only if it rarely loses
cards.brief: Speculation wins when the miss rate p is below (ts−tf)/(ts−tf+Cd). A 1 ns fast path against a 5 ns generic path means p must be about 1e-4 to 1e-3. The IC is linear up to 4 Maps, then hashed.

cards.title: Speculation is only safe because deopt is always there
cards.brief: Remove any piece and it breaks: no Maps means hash lookups, no ICs means a lookup forever, and speculation without deopt is unsound. Deopt is the safety net that makes aggressive guards legal. Real call sites see one shape more than 90% of the time.

cards.title: Poly limit 4, dictionary mode, and 21 elements kinds
cards.brief: A smaller poly limit goes megamorphic sooner, and a larger one slows every check. delete drops an object to dictionary mode, where ICs can't specialize. Elements kinds only generalize one way. The cap of 4 is an engineering choice, not derived.

cards.title: Optimizer Map bugs have repeatedly become type confusion
cards.brief: When the compiler removes a CheckMaps, it has proved the Map can't change. A wrong side-effect model gives type confusion, then addrof, then arbitrary read and write. CVE-2020-6418, CVE-2020-16009 and CVE-2025-2135 follow that pattern. The V8 sandbox contains these; it does not fix them.

cards.title: Real engines add tiers and deviate from textbook PICs
cards.brief: Maglev compiles about 10× slower than Sparkplug and 10× faster than TurboFan, and cut Speedometer energy by 10%. Turboshaft halved compile time. V8's ICs live in a heap feedback vector, not patched machine code, and megamorphic sites use a global stub cache.

cards.title: Recent work keeps speculation sound and cheap
cards.brief: Mutable heap numbers (2025) avoid an allocation per update, about 2.5× on async-fs. Turboshaft's CFG IR halved compile time. Translation validation and fuzzers (TurboTV, OptFuzz, DUMPLING) hunt the optimizer bugs that keep recurring.

cards.title: Sound speculation, containment and warm-up are still open
cards.brief: No production-scale proof says effect-chain Map inference is correct, and the same bug family recurs from 2020 to 2025. Open questions: can the sandbox make JIT bugs non-critical, can feedback be cached without staleness, and does IC state leak timing?

cards.title: Inline caches date to 1984, and V8 added Maglev in 2023
cards.brief: Smalltalk-80 inline caching (1984), Self maps (1989), polymorphic ICs (1991), V8 hidden classes (2008), then Ignition and TurboFan (2017), Sparkplug (2021), Maglev (2023), and Turboshaft with the sandbox (2024–25).

cards.title: A 30-second script shows Maps, deopts and IC timing
cards.brief: Run node --allow-natives-syntax ic_demo.js. It prints Map sharing, dictionary mode after delete, and mono and poly and mega timings: 0.99, 4.06 and 4.90 ns per call on one machine, one noisy run.

cards.title: Test yourself
cards.brief: 20 questions across mechanism, why, counterfactual, adversarial, connection and open. Answers reveal on click.

cards.title: Three follow-ups: sandbox, Turboshaft IR, CacheIR
cards.brief: The V8 sandbox and its code-pointer tables, Sea of Nodes to Turboshaft, and SpiderMonkey's CacheIR, which shares one IR between the interpreter and the compiler.

cards.title: Papers, V8 source and the CVE writeups behind each claim
cards.brief: Papers (PICs, TurboTV, OptFuzz, DUMPLING, CacheIR, POPL '21), V8 source and blog posts, and the Project Zero, Zellic and GitHub writeups. Items the research notes never opened are marked.

cold.q: One read site sees four object shapes instead of one. How much slower is each read?
cold.reveal: About 4×. 4.06 ns against 0.99 ns in my run on Node 24.12, one noisy run. Eight shapes cost about the same, 4.90 ns, because the global stub cache takes over.

order.q: Do {x: 1, y: 2} and {y: 2, x: 1} share a Map?
options: Yes, same keys means same Map
No, the order of additions sets the Map
order.reveal: No. Map transitions are labelled by property name in insertion order, so the second literal takes a different branch and ends at a different Map. Two Maps at one site make it polymorphic.

breakeven.q: A fast path costs 1 ns and the generic path 5 ns. How rarely can the guard fail for speculation to pay off?
breakeven.reveal: About 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 10,000 (p between 1e-4 and 1e-3). A deopt costs much more than a load, so a bet that misses often loses. The break-even formula is in the math section.

cves.q: How many of the CVEs in the security section come from a wrong Map assumption in optimized code?
cves.reveal: 3. CVE-2020-6418, CVE-2020-16009 and CVE-2025-2135. Each one is a wrong fact about Maps or elements kinds that removed a guard. The Super IC bug (CVE-2022-1134) is listed separately and is not counted here.

maglev.q: How many times slower than Sparkplug does Maglev compile code?
maglev.reveal: About 10×, and about 10× faster than TurboFan, per the V8 Maglev post. An earlier research note said 20×; the primary source says 10×.

questions.q: What exactly is in a JSObject's first three words?
questions.a: Map pointer, properties (overflow backing store), elements. In-object fields follow; with pointer compression each is 4 bytes, so the first field is at offset 12.

questions.q: What does a monomorphic LoadIC slot contain after the first miss?
questions.a: A weak reference to the Map plus a handler (typically a Smi encoding kind, in-object flag, double flag and field index).

questions.q: What happens on getX({y:1,x:2}) after getX was optimized for {x,y}?
questions.a: CheckMaps fails, then eager deopt rebuilds the Ignition frame, the IC becomes polymorphic, and a later reopt uses a 2-way check.

questions.q: How does push(1.5) on a Smi array change things?
questions.a: The Map changes to PACKED_DOUBLE_ELEMENTS and the backing store is rewritten as unboxed doubles. The change is one-way.

questions.q: Where does a megamorphic site look?
questions.a: The global two-level stub cache, keyed on (Map, name). On a miss it falls back to a runtime lookup.

questions.q: Why do {x,y} and {y,x} have different Maps?
questions.a: Transitions are labelled by property name in insertion order, and offsets depend on that order.

questions.q: Why cap polymorphism at 4?
questions.a: Linear checks cost more per entry while the hit-rate gain levels off. Beyond that, a hashed global lookup is cheaper. It is an engineering constant.

questions.q: Why is deoptimization necessary rather than a luxury?
questions.a: Guards can fail. Without a way back to a generic tier, the optimized code would have to be correct for all inputs, which defeats speculation.

questions.q: Why does delete hurt later reads?
questions.a: The object flips to dictionary mode. It has no stable Map to key on, so ICs can't specialize.

questions.q: What if V8 never removed redundant CheckMaps?
questions.a: The CVE-2020-6418 class mostly disappears, but every property access pays a compare, which loses a chunk of optimized-code speed.

questions.q: What if the IC cap were 1?
questions.a: Any two-shape site would go megamorphic. The common optional-field pattern would hit the stub cache constantly.

questions.q: What if elements kinds could transition back?
questions.a: Optimized code would need more dependencies and deopts, and flip-flopping arrays would thrash. One-way transitions keep the lattice finite and monotone.

questions.q: How does an attacker turn a missing side-effect model into addrof?
questions.a: They use user-controllable code (a Proxy, valueOf) at the unmodeled effect to change the Map or elements kind. The optimized code still reads with the old layout, so a double array's words are read as tagged pointers (a leak), or a crafted double is read as a pointer (a fake object).

questions.q: Can an attacker influence what the IC caches?
questions.a: Yes. They control which shapes reach a site, so they steer the feedback and therefore which speculation the compiler makes. This is JIT-spray-like feedback grooming.

questions.q: Why doesn't the V8 sandbox end this class?
questions.a: It bounds what corrupted pointers can reach, not the corruption itself. In-sandbox arbitrary read and write remains, and escapes target the boundary.

questions.q: How is this like a CPU branch predictor plus a pipeline flush?
questions.a: The guard is a predicted branch and the deopt is the flush. Both bet on regularity and trade a rare large penalty for a common cheap path.

questions.q: How do Shapes in SpiderMonkey differ?
questions.a: The idea is the same. ICs are expressed as CacheIR, so the same IR can be interpreted or compiled.

questions.q: How does this relate to Spectre-style attacks?
questions.a: Both are speculation: one in hardware, one in software. Software speculation's guards are architecturally visible bugs, while hardware's are microarchitectural leaks.

questions.q: Can speculative JIT optimizations be formally verified at production scale?
questions.a: Unsettled. Translation validation finds bugs but does not yet gate production releases.

questions.q: Can feedback be persisted safely across loads?
questions.a: Unsettled. It trades warm-up for staleness and attacker-influenceable state.

own-map-tree.caption: Follow the two branches: the same fields added in a different order walk a different path and end at a different Map (M2 versus M3).

own-object-slack.caption: Look at the reserved slack: fields that fit stay at a fixed offset in the object, and the overflow field takes one extra pointer hop.

own-ic-states.caption: The IC state only moves rightward: once a site is polymorphic or megamorphic, it never returns to monomorphic.

own-deopt-flow.caption: Trace the failed guard from optimized code to the interpreter, then to a polymorphic IC and a recompile that guards on both Maps.

own-elements-lattice.caption: Arrows only point right or down, so a packed array that gets a hole or a double never returns to its earlier kind.

own-order-maps.caption: Same keys in a different order give two Maps at one site, so the site is polymorphic even though the code looks identical.

own-cve-chain.caption: Each step relies on a fact the optimizer must model; one wrong fact removes a guard, and the rest of the chain follows.
